title: The Two Beggars at the Golden Gate (TA)
summary: One beggar prays to the Emperor for help, while the other prays to God. Akbar rewards the first beggar, but destiny delivers the gold to the second. [TA]
full_text:
Outside the main gate of the Agra Fort, two blind beggars sat begging every morning.

The first beggar shouted whenever the Emperor's retinue passed: 'May God bless Emperor Akbar! He who receives the favor of the Emperor receives the wealth of the world!'

The second beggar chanted calmly: 'May God bless all creation! He who relies upon the Almighty Creator is never in need of anything!'

Akbar, hearing both men daily, felt his royal pride stirred by the first beggar's praise: 'That first beggar acknowledges my imperial power! I shall reward his loyalty and show him that the Emperor can make a man rich in an instant!'

Akbar ordered the palace baker to bake a large loaf of sweet bread. Inside the dough, the royal jeweler concealed ten heavy gold mohurs.

Akbar personally handed the loaf to the first beggar, saying: 'Take this bread, my friend; it will satisfy your hunger!'

The first beggar felt the heavy bread, thanked the Emperor, and sat down. Being already full from a bowl of porridge, he turned to the second beggar and said:

'Brother, the Emperor gave me this heavy loaf of bread, but I am not hungry. If you give me two copper dams, you may have this entire loaf of bread for your dinner.'

The second beggar agreed, gave his two copper coins, took the loaf of bread, and walked home.

When the second beggar broke open the bread at his hut, out rolled ten gleaming gold mohurs! Rejoicing in God's providence, the second beggar bought a house, cattle, and farmland, and was never in want again.

The next morning, Akbar saw the first beggar sitting in the dust, still begging!

Akbar stopped in shock: 'Did you not eat the bread I gave you yesterday?'

The beggar replied: 'No, Sire, I sold it to my blind companion for two copper dams!'

Birbal smiled with gentle, profound wisdom:

'You see, Your Majesty? Man proposes, but God disposes!

'You sought to enrich the man who relied upon your royal favor, but destiny delivered the treasure directly into the hands of the man who trusted in the Almighty!

'An emperor can bestow bread, but only providence can grant the fortune within.'

Akbar bowed his head in deep humility, acknowledging that human power is merely an instrument of a higher divine will.
moral: நீதி மற்றும் வாழ்க்கை பாடம்: Wit beats power
